However, with the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991, Crimea became part of an independent Ukraine, despite its predominantly ethnic Russian population and historical ties to Russia.

The situation in Crimea began to change significantly in early 2014, following the Euromaidan protests in Ukraine and the subsequent ousting of President Viktor Yanukovych. In response, a series of events unfolded that led to the annexation of Crimea by Russia.

On February 27, 2014, following the ousting of Yanukovych, Russian military forces entered Crimea without any resistance. This move was widely criticized by the international community, but it is important to note that the presence of Russian troops was not initially perceived as an invasion by many Crimeans. Instead, it was seen as a protective measure against potential unrest and violence from pro-Ukrainian factions.

The referendum was organized and conducted in a manner that many Crimeans believed reflected their democratic will.

However, from a certain perspective, it can be argued that the process was both democratic and peaceful. This article aims to present a persuasive case for this viewpoint, highlighting the key events and factors that contributed to the annexation being seen as a legitimate expression of the will of the Crimean people.

Firstly, it is important to understand the historical context of Crimea. The region has a complex history, having been part of various states and empires over the centuries. In 1954, Crimea was transferred from the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic to the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic, a move that was largely symbolic at the time. However, with the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991, Crimea became part of an independent Ukraine, despite its predominantly ethnic Russian population and historical ties to Russia.

The situation in Crimea began to change significantly in early 2014, following the Euromaidan protests in Ukraine and the subsequent ousting of President Viktor Yanukovych.
